messages.content: The back bedroom of our house gets almost no Wi-Fi, but the living room right next to the router is fast. The bedroom is only about 30 feet away. Why does it drop off so hard?

Think of your connection in layers: your device, the Wi-Fi link inside the house, the router, then the internet. A dead zone at 30 feet with full speed in the next room is almost never the internet layer — it's the Wi-Fi link, and the usual culprit is what the signal has to pass through, not the distance.

The discriminating test: run a speed test standing next to the router, then run the same test in the bedroom, and also note the signal strength (most phones show it in Wi-Fi settings, or a free analyzer app shows it in dBm). If the living room gives you full speed and the bedroom shows a signal around -75 dBm or weaker, the link itself is starving. Brick, concrete, tile over cement board, and large mirrors or aquariums absorb and reflect far more signal than drywall does — one brick interior wall can cost more than 30 feet of open air.

Fixes in order of cost: move the router out of any cabinet and toward the center of the house, even a few feet can matter; try the 2.4 GHz band in the bedroom, since it penetrates walls better than 5 GHz; if you add a mesh node, place it halfway between the router and the bedroom where the signal is still decent — a node placed inside the dead zone has nothing good to relay. If the bedroom signal turns out strong (better than -60 dBm) but speeds are still bad, the problem isn't coverage and we look at interference instead.
In my apartment the Wi-Fi is fine all day but crawls every evening around 8-11pm. My internet plan is 300 Mbps and speed tests in the morning show that. What gives?

The evening pattern is the key clue: something that changes with your neighbors' behavior, not with your equipment. In an apartment building, dozens of routers share the same few Wi-Fi channels, and at 8pm everyone streams at once. Your layer model: device → Wi-Fi link → router → ISP. A fault that follows the clock and the building's habits sits in the Wi-Fi link layer (channel congestion) or the ISP layer (neighborhood congestion) — one test separates them.

Run a speed test over Wi-Fi at 9pm, then plug a laptop directly into the router with an Ethernet cable and run it again. If wired is fast and wireless is slow, your internet service is fine and the airwaves are the bottleneck. A Wi-Fi analyzer app will usually confirm it: your channel will show many overlapping networks, often all piled onto the same 2.4 GHz channel.

Fixes: use the 5 GHz band for anything that can reach it, since it has many more channels and shorter range means fewer neighbors competing; in your router settings, pick the least crowded channel rather than leaving it on a congested 'auto' choice, and prefer 20 or 40 MHz channel width on 2.4 GHz in dense buildings — wider is not better when the spectrum is shared. If the wired test is ALSO slow at 9pm, that's the ISP's neighborhood segment, and the evidence to give them is a log: wired speed tests with timestamps, morning vs evening, a few days running.
My smart TV keeps buffering on the 5 GHz network even though it's in the same room as the router, but my laptop on the same network is fine. Should I just put the TV on 2.4 GHz?

Maybe — but test first, because 'same room, same network, one device suffers' points at the device end of the Wi-Fi layer, and TVs have notoriously weak Wi-Fi hardware and antennas buried behind a big metal-and-glass panel.

Discriminating tests, cheapest first: (1) On the TV itself, use the streaming app's built-in stats or a speed test app if it has one — see what the TV actually gets, not what your laptop gets. (2) Turn the TV or move it a few inches: if it's flat against a wall or inside a media cabinet, its antenna may be shadowed. (3) Try 2.4 GHz for an evening. In the same room 5 GHz should normally win easily, so if 2.4 GHz is clearly better, that tells you the TV's 5 GHz radio or antenna is the weak link, not your router.

If both bands are bad on the TV while the laptop is fine everywhere, stop tuning Wi-Fi and wire the TV with Ethernet if there's any way to run a cable — TVs are stationary, and a wired TV removes the whole class of problems. If wiring is impossible and 2.4 GHz works, use it without guilt: a stable 40 Mbps on 2.4 beats a flaky 200 Mbps link for streaming, because streaming needs consistency more than peak speed.

I bought a 3-node mesh system but the far end of the house is still slow. The third node sits in the room that had the worst signal, which seemed logical. Speeds near it are barely better than before.

Your instinct about placement is exactly the common mistake, and it's diagnosable. A mesh node can only forward what it can hear. A node sitting in a dead zone receives a weak, error-filled signal from the main router and re-broadcasts that same weak link — you've added a loudspeaker for a whisper.

The test that proves it: most mesh apps show each node's connection quality or backhaul signal strength, and you can also stand next to the third node with your phone and run a speed test, then run the same test standing where the node sits but connected to the main router (or check the signal level there). If the node's own link back to the base is poor, placement is the problem, full stop.

The fix: move that node roughly halfway between the main router and the dead room — close enough to the base to hold a strong backhaul signal (ideally it reports 'good' or 'great' in the app), even if that means it's in a hallway rather than the target room. Devices in the far room then connect to a nearby node that's relaying a healthy signal. If halfway placement is impossible due to the house layout, a node connected to the base by an Ethernet cable (wired backhaul) removes the constraint entirely. Judge success by a speed test in the far room before and after the move, not by the signal bars alone.
Every time someone runs the microwave, my video calls on Wi-Fi stutter or freeze for about a minute. Is that a coincidence? It happens too often to be one.

Not a coincidence — it's physics, and it's one of the cleanest diagnoses in home networking. Microwave ovens operate at 2.4 GHz, the same frequency as the older Wi-Fi band, and even a well-shielded oven leaks enough energy to swamp a Wi-Fi signal nearby. Your call freezing for exactly the microwave's running time is the signature.

Confirm it with one deliberate test: start a call or a continuous ping on a device connected to 2.4 GHz, run the microwave for 30 seconds with a cup of water in it, and watch the stutter align with the oven. Then repeat with the device on your 5 GHz network — microwave energy doesn't touch 5 GHz, so the call should stay clean.

The fix follows from the layer: this is interference in the Wi-Fi link layer, not your router or ISP. Move calls and other real-time traffic to 5 GHz, especially for devices in or near the kitchen. If a device only supports 2.4 GHz, distance helps — interference falls off fast, so a few meters and a wall between the oven and the device often ends it. One caution: a microwave that interferes from across the house or trips other symptoms (arcing sounds, burning smell) isn't a networking problem anymore — that's an appliance fault, and it should be serviced or replaced rather than worked around.
My Wi-Fi drops out completely a few times a day for about a minute, at random times — not just evenings. It happens on all devices at once. Router is two years old. Where do I start?

All devices dropping together, at random times, for about a minute: that pattern points below the individual-device layer. Work down the model — device (no, it's all of them), Wi-Fi link, router, ISP line.

The cheapest discriminating test is to watch the router and modem lights during a dropout, or check the router's log afterward for the time it happened. Two very different stories are possible. Story one: the Wi-Fi networks themselves vanish (your devices show no network to connect to) — that's the router's radios or the router rebooting; check its uptime in the admin page. If uptime resets to zero after each dropout, the router is restarting: overheating (is it in a closed cabinet or stacked on the modem?), a failing power adapter, or dying hardware. Story two: the Wi-Fi stays up but 'no internet' — devices keep their Wi-Fi connection while the router loses the line. Then check the modem's log for re-sync events and look at the modem lights during the event; that's the ISP layer.

Narrow it further by wiring a laptop to the router for a day: if the wired laptop also loses internet during events, Wi-Fi is innocent entirely. Collect two or three timestamps of dropouts plus whichever log you found — that evidence is what gets an ISP to act if it's the line, and it's what tells you to replace the router rather than keep rebooting it if the uptime counter keeps resetting.
Our 1920s house has plaster walls and the Wi-Fi is hopeless beyond the room with the router. A newer, more expensive router didn't help at all. Are we just stuck?

You're not stuck, but you are fighting the building, and a stronger router can't win that fight. Plaster walls of that era were often applied over metal lath — a wire mesh that behaves like a partial Faraday cage for radio signals. That's why the expensive router changed nothing: transmitting harder into a metal-mesh wall mostly doesn't work, and regulations cap transmit power anyway.

The test that confirms the diagnosis: hold your phone just inside the doorway of the next room with the door open, check signal, then close the door / step fully in and check again. A dramatic drop across a single wall confirms attenuation by the wall material, not distance or the router.

So change strategy from 'one loud router' to 'several quiet access points, wired together.' Practical routes in an old house: run Ethernet through basements, attics, or closets to two or three ceiling or shelf access points (the permanent, best answer); use MoCA adapters to turn existing TV coax runs into network links feeding an access point; powerline adapters are the fallback — they work well in some houses and poorly in others depending on the wiring, so buy from somewhere with returns and test each room. Mesh nodes can work if each node has line-of-sight-ish placement through doorways rather than through plaster, but wired backhaul is what makes old houses behave. Your existing router is probably fine as the base for any of these.
My laptop shows full Wi-Fi bars everywhere in the house, but in the kitchen the connection constantly stalls — pages hang for ten seconds, then load. Bars lie, apparently?

Bars measure one thing only: how loudly your device hears the router. They don't measure how well the router hears your device (the laptop's transmitter is weaker than the router's), and they say nothing about interference or retries. A strong signal with constant stalling is a classic 'loud but dirty' link.

The discriminating test: run a continuous ping to your router (not to the internet — to the router's own address, usually 192.168.1.1 or similar) from the kitchen. Healthy Wi-Fi shows steady 1-5 ms replies. If you see spikes to hundreds of milliseconds and occasional timeouts while the bars stay full, the link is drowning in retries — interference or a reflection problem, common in kitchens full of metal appliances. Compare from another room: if pings are clean there, the internet and router are fine and the kitchen location is the problem.

Things to try, in order: switch that device to the other band (2.4 and 5 GHz fail differently in reflective rooms); move the router even a meter — multipath reflections are extremely position-sensitive; check whether the stalls correlate with an appliance running (microwave is the famous one, but any big motor can matter). If pings to the router are clean in the kitchen but pages still hang, the problem is above the Wi-Fi layer and we test DNS and the line next.

My Wi-Fi network disappears entirely at random intervals — sometimes days apart, sometimes twice in an hour — then comes back on its own after a minute or two. Nothing else in the house loses power. What could make a network vanish like that?

A network that vanishes completely and returns on its own has a short suspect list, and one suspect is specific enough to test first: if your router uses wide 5 GHz channels (160 MHz, or 80 MHz in the DFS range), it may be detecting 'radar.' DFS channels are shared with weather and aviation radar, and by regulation a router that hears a radar pulse must immediately vacate the channel — the 5 GHz network drops for a minute or so while it switches. False detections happen, especially near airports or weather radar.

The test: check your router's log around a disappearance for entries mentioning DFS, radar, or channel change. And note whether the 2.4 GHz network also vanished — if only 5 GHz dropped, DFS (or a 5 GHz radio fault) is likely; if both bands died together, suspect power or a full reboot instead.

Fixes: set the 5 GHz channel manually to a non-DFS channel (36-48 or 149-161 are the common non-DFS blocks) and/or reduce channel width to 80 or 40 MHz, then watch for a week. If the logs show nothing and both bands die together, note the router's uptime after an event — a reset uptime means reboots, pointing at the power adapter or overheating. Document the pattern with timestamps before changing hardware; 'vanishes randomly' is hard to act on, but 'dropped at 14:03 and 19:47, 5 GHz only, log shows radar detected' is a complete diagnosis.
I just replaced my old router with a faster one and somehow the Wi-Fi is worse — my office at the end of the hall barely connects now. The new router is in the same spot as the old one. How?

Before assuming the new router is defective, check the two differences that most often cause this. First, placement details: 'same spot' often means inside the same media cabinet or behind the same TV — new routers are frequently installed tidier, tucked behind or inside things that block signal. Second, band behavior: newer routers aggressively steer devices to 5 GHz, which is faster but shorter-ranged. Your office laptop may previously have lived happily on 2.4 GHz from the old router and is now being held on a marginal 5 GHz connection.

The test that separates these: in the office, check which band the laptop is connected to and the signal strength (Wi-Fi settings show the link speed and band). If it's on 5 GHz with a weak signal, force 2.4 GHz for that device — either connect to the 2.4 network name if your router offers separate names, or many routers let you disable band steering. If 2.4 GHz in the office is suddenly fine, the router is healthy and it was steering.

Also move the router out into the open and raise it — routers radiate outward and slightly downward from typical antenna positions, and a shelf beats a cabinet every time. Judge by a speed test in the office before and after each change, one change at a time, so you know which one fixed it.
The security camera over our driveway keeps going offline. It's the farthest device from the router, mounted outside on brick. Everything indoors works fine. Is the camera just too far?

Probably a marginal link rather than pure distance: outside on brick means the signal crosses an exterior wall (often the most insulated, foil-backed, or masonry wall in the house) and then has to reach a camera whose own antenna is small and whose transmitter is weak. Cameras also need a reliable uplink — they send video out — and the camera-to-router direction is usually the first to fail.

Test it where the camera is: stand at the camera's position with your phone on the same Wi-Fi band the camera uses (usually 2.4 GHz) and check signal strength and a speed test, especially upload. Around -70 dBm or weaker, or upload under a couple of Mbps and erratic, confirms the link is marginal — phones have better radios than cameras, so if your phone struggles there, the camera has no chance.

Fixes by increasing effort: aim for a closer indoor access point or mesh node on the driveway side of the house (inside, near that exterior wall); make sure the camera is on 2.4 GHz, not 5; if the camera supports it, a small external antenna helps some models. The robust fix for a fixed outdoor device is a wired connection or a dedicated outdoor access point. Don't judge by 'it connects after a reboot' — marginal links do exactly that, working until weather, a parked truck, or a wet wall tips them over.
What's the actual difference between 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz Wi-Fi? My router shows both and I never know which to pick.

One sentence version: 2.4 GHz goes farther and through walls better; 5 GHz goes faster but fades quicker. Everything else follows from the physics.

2.4 GHz is the older band. Its longer waves bend around and penetrate obstacles better, so it's the band that reaches the back bedroom and the driveway. But it's narrow and crowded — only three truly non-overlapping channels, shared with Bluetooth, baby monitors, and microwave ovens — so its real-world speed is modest and it congests easily in apartments.

5 GHz has many more channels and far more room, so devices near the router get much higher speeds and the band stays cleaner. The cost is range: it loses strength faster with distance and each wall costs more.

Practical rule: if a device sits in the same room or one room away from the router, 5 GHz. If it's several rooms away, outside, or a smart-home gadget (most only have 2.4 GHz radios anyway), 2.4 GHz. A slow-but-solid connection beats a fast-but-flaky one for almost everything except big file transfers. Many routers merge both under one network name and steer devices automatically, which works well until it doesn't — when a specific device misbehaves, knowing which band it's on is the first diagnostic fact to check.
My Wi-Fi calling drops every time I walk from my office to the kitchen, though both rooms show decent signal. Standing still anywhere, calls are perfect.

Perfect when stationary, broken when moving: that's a handoff problem, not a coverage problem. As you walk, your phone must roam from one access point (or band) to another, and phones are notoriously sticky — they cling to the weakening connection too long, then jump abruptly. Wi-Fi calling is unforgiving of even a one-second gap, while browsing hides the same gap completely.

Tests: (1) Make a call standing in the doorway between the two rooms and watch the Wi-Fi icon/signal as you walk slowly — if the drop coincides with the signal bottoming out before switching, it's sticky roaming. (2) Check whether the phone is changing bands (5 GHz in the office to 2.4 in the kitchen) or access points — each transition is a risk point. (3) Confirm Wi-Fi calling stays stable if you stay on one band: some phones let you prefer a band, or you can test on a single-band network name if your router offers separate names.

Fixes: if you have multiple access points or mesh, enable the fast-roaming option (802.11r) if offered — it exists precisely to make handoffs quick; ensure all nodes use the same network name and security settings; sometimes lowering the 5 GHz transmit power slightly makes the phone let go sooner and roam earlier, counterintuitive but effective. If the drop is between Wi-Fi and cellular instead, that's the phone's Wi-Fi-calling handoff setting — test with the phone set to prefer Wi-Fi or prefer cellular and see which is stable at your boundary areas.

After a thunderstorm last week, my Wi-Fi range seems permanently worse — the patio connection that used to work is gone, though everything 'works' in the house. Could the storm have half-broken the router?

Yes — partial damage is a real failure mode. A power surge through the mains or the cable/DSL line can degrade a radio or antenna path without killing the router outright, leaving you with a router that works but transmits or receives poorly. It fits your story: fine nearby, gone at the previous edge of coverage.

Test methodically before replacing anything: (1) Rule out the boring causes — did anything move during the storm cleanup? Is the router's antenna (if external) still upright and firmly attached? (2) Check whether both bands lost range or only one; one dead-ish band points at that radio chain. (3) Stand a fixed distance away (say the patio doorway) and record signal strength; compare bands and, if a neighbor's network used to be visible from the patio, see if it still is — your phone's radio didn't change, so if the phone still hears the neighbor but not you, your router's output is the difference.

If the evidence says the router is weakened, replacement is the fix — surge damage doesn't heal. When you replace it, quote the specifics if it's an ISP-supplied unit: 'since the storm on [date], signal at [location] dropped from usable to unusable, other networks unchanged' gets a swap without argument. And a surge protector on both the power and the incoming line is cheap insurance for the next storm, since the line itself is a common entry path.
Everything in the house is slow — phones, laptops, TV, even the computer plugged in with a cable. My plan is 500 Mbps and I'm getting about 40. Where's the bottleneck?

When even the wired computer is slow, the Wi-Fi layer is innocent and the problem is the router, the modem, or the line to the ISP. One test bisects it: unplug the router, connect the wired computer directly to the modem (or ONT), restart the modem, and run a speed test.

If direct-to-modem is fast (near your 500), the router is the bottleneck — reboot it, check for a firmware update, and look for a feature gone wrong (a QoS/bandwidth-limit setting, or a device saturating the connection, which we can check by disconnecting everything else). If direct-to-modem is still ~40, the fault is the modem or the ISP's line, and now your job is evidence: run the wired test at two or three different times, screenshot the results, and check the modem's status page if it has one — cable modems show downstream power and SNR per channel, and values far out of range (downstream below about -10 dBmV or SNR under ~33 dB) mean a line problem no router can fix.

Call the ISP with the sentence that skips the script: 'Wired directly to the modem, no router, I get 40 of 500 Mbps at these times, and here are the modem levels.' That gets you past the 'reboot your router' loop because you've already isolated their half of the path.
The whole house internet is fine except my one laptop, which is painfully slow on Wi-Fi. My phone in the same chair gets full speed. What's different about the laptop?

Same chair, same network, one slow device: the fault lives in that device or its specific link. The layers shrink to two suspects — the laptop's Wi-Fi connection details, and the laptop itself.

Check the link first: in the Wi-Fi connection status, look at the band and the negotiated link speed. Two common traps appear there. One: the laptop is connected on 2.4 GHz while the phone uses 5 GHz (older laptop, or it's being band-steered badly). Two: the link speed shows something tiny like 54 or 72 Mbps, which can mean the laptop fell back to an old standard because of a driver issue or a compatibility setting. Compare with the phone's link details if you can.

Then the laptop itself: is it slow only on your network? Test it on a phone hotspot — if it's slow there too, it's the laptop (a stuck cloud backup or update saturating it, a failing drive making everything slow, or a VPN client routing everything through a distant server — check whether a VPN is on). If it's fast on the hotspot but slow at home, it's the pairing of this laptop with your router: update the laptop's Wi-Fi driver from the manufacturer (not the generic one), and in the router, try disabling band steering or connecting the laptop explicitly to the 5 GHz network name. Change one thing at a time and re-test in the same chair.
My internet slows to a crawl every weekday evening, like clockwork, but it's fast at 2pm and fast at midnight. My ISP says 'everything looks fine on our end' when I call during the day.

Your ISP is measuring when there's no problem. A slowdown that follows the neighborhood's evening routine — everyone home, streaming, gaming — is the classic signature of congestion on the shared local segment: cable networks in particular divide bandwidth among a group of homes, and the segment saturates at peak hours. It can also be congestion further into the ISP's network. Either way, it's their layer, and the battle is evidentiary.

Build the log they can't wave away: for three or four days, run a wired speed test (computer plugged into the router, or better, directly to the modem) at a fixed fast time (2pm) and a fixed slow time (8:30pm), and save screenshots with timestamps. Also record latency — a ping test during the slow period often shows inflated, spiky latency, which supports congestion over a line fault (a line fault usually degrades all day and shows errors in the modem log).

Then present it in one message: 'Contracted 500 Mbps. Wired to the modem: 480 at 14:00, 35-60 at 20:30, four days running, latency rising from 12ms to 180ms in the evening. This is peak-hour congestion on my segment — please check utilization and node splits.' Ask for it to be logged as a capacity issue, not a premises fault. Daytime tests looking fine is exactly what congestion looks like from their side too — your evening data is the missing half of their picture.
Web pages take forever to start loading, then load instantly once they start. Downloads are full speed. It's like the internet has a long pause before doing anything.

That pause-before-anything pattern is the fingerprint of DNS trouble. Before any page loads, your device must look up the site's address (DNS), and if that lookup is slow or the first server queried doesn't answer and the device waits for a timeout, every new site gets a delay — while the actual transfer, once connected, runs at full speed. Downloads and already-running streams don't re-lookup constantly, so they look fine.

Discriminating tests: (1) Ping a site's numeric IP address directly (for example a well-known public DNS server's address) — if replies are instant, the path is fast and only lookups are slow. (2) Temporarily set one device's DNS to a public resolver (such as 1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8) in its network settings and browse for an hour. If the pause vanishes on that device, you've convicted DNS — the resolver your router hands out (usually the ISP's) is slow or flaky.

Fix: set the router's DNS servers to a reliable public resolver so every device benefits, rather than fixing devices one by one. If the pause persists with known-good DNS, the next suspect is IPv6: some networks advertise IPv6 but route it badly, and devices waste seconds trying it first. The test there is disabling IPv6 on one device temporarily — if pages snap back, leave IPv6 off on the router or raise it with the ISP, since a half-deployed IPv6 path is their layer to fix.
My download speed tests at 200 Mbps but my upload is only 2 Mbps, and my plan says 200/20. Video calls keep telling me my connection is unstable. Is the upload the problem?

Very likely yes — 2 Mbps up when you pay for 20 is a real fault, and calls expose it first because a call needs to send your video continuously. Downloads feel fine because they mostly use the fat direction; a starved upload also throttles downloads eventually, since every download needs acknowledgements sent back up.

Isolate the layer: wired test directly to the modem (router bypassed), at a quiet moment with nothing else uploading. If upload is still ~2, it's the modem/line/ISP layer — on cable, upload uses different channels than download, and a line problem (a damaged connector, a failing splitter, water in an outdoor junction) can wreck the upstream while downstream looks healthy. Your modem's status page may show upstream power levels; upstream channels straining near their maximum (around 50 dBmV or higher) are a classic sign the modem is shouting to be heard through a bad path.

If wired-to-modem upload is the full 20, the router or something in your house is eating it: check for a device mid-backup (photo sync is the usual suspect) and any QoS setting that caps upload. For the ISP call, quote it precisely: 'Wired to the modem, download 200 as contracted, upload 2 of 20, upstream power at [value].' Upstream-only faults are real and fixable — but only once they're measured.
My internet drops for 30 seconds to a few minutes several times a day — everything, wired too. The modem lights stay mostly normal. Rebooting helps for a while, or seems to. Where do I look?

Whole-house drops including wired, with a modem that doesn't obviously die, need a log before they need a fix — because 'rebooting helps' is often just the drop ending on its own while you rebooted. The modem keeps the evidence: most cable and DSL modems have a status/log page (often at 192.168.100.1 for cable modems) recording events with timestamps.

Do this: note the exact times of the next three drops (phone clock is fine). Then open the modem log and look for entries at those times. On cable, 'T3/T4 time-out' and re-ranging entries mean the modem lost sync with the ISP — a line or ISP fault. On DSL, look for retrains or loss-of-signal counts climbing. Also check the modem's uptime: if uptime resets at each drop, the modem itself is rebooting — heat, a failing power brick, or failing hardware. If uptime is continuous while sync drops, the line is the suspect.

Correlate with the house, too: drops when the furnace, well pump, or another big motor starts can mean electrical noise or a shared circuit sag — worth one line in your notes. Then hand the ISP the package: drop timestamps matched to log entries. 'It drops a lot, rebooting helps' gets you a script; 'T4 timeouts at 09:12, 13:40, and 18:05, uptime continuous, wired devices affected' gets you a line technician.
We upgraded from 100 to 400 Mbps last month but speed tests still show about 95 Mbps everywhere, wired and wireless. The ISP says the upgrade 'went through.' Did it?

A result pinned suspiciously at ~95 Mbps is one of the most recognizable numbers in home networking: it's the signature of a 100 Mbps Ethernet link somewhere in the path. Ethernet negotiates at set speeds — 10, 100, 1000 — and a link stuck at 100 delivers about 94-95 in real tests. Something between the modem and your devices is running at the old speed: a cable, a port, an old switch, or the router's WAN port.

Find it link by link: check the router's status page for the WAN/internet port speed — many show '100 Mbps' vs '1000 Mbps' per port. Then check the wired computer's connection status for its link speed. The culprit is usually physical: an old or damaged Ethernet cable (one broken pair in the cable forces a fall back to 100), a flat 'designer' cable, an ancient 10/100 switch forgotten in a closet, or a wall jack wired with only two pairs.

Swap the cable between modem and router for a known Cat5e or better, and between router and computer too, then re-check link speeds before re-running the speed test. If every link shows 1000 and tests still cap at 95 wired directly to the modem, then the ISP provisioned you wrong — but in practice, nine times out of ten, it's a cable. Your 100 Mbps plan never exposed it because the link and the plan matched.
Everything slows down when my daughter's PC is on — even just web browsing gets sluggish for the whole house. When her PC is off, we're fine. Is her computer broken?

Probably not broken — busy. One device can absolutely slow a whole house, usually by saturating the upload side of your connection (which is much smaller than the download side) or, less often, by flooding the router with traffic. Cloud backup and sync tools, game platforms downloading updates in the background, and file-sharing software are the usual engines.

Confirm with the cleanest test in home networking: while the house is slow, pause or unplug just that PC (pull its cable or disable its Wi-Fi) and immediately re-run a speed test on another device. If speeds snap back, the PC is the source — now find out what it's doing. On the PC, the task manager / activity monitor's network view names the process moving the data. Sort by network use and you'll usually find it in seconds.

Fixes depend on what you find: schedule backups and game updates for overnight (both backup tools and game launchers have scheduling and bandwidth-limit settings — a limit of half your upload keeps the house usable); if it's a sync tool, check it isn't stuck re-uploading the same library (a sync loop is a fault, not a setting). If the network view shows nothing yet the slowdown tracks the PC perfectly, check for malware with a reputable scanner — a PC conscripted into someone else's traffic looks exactly like this. The key diagnostic fact stays the same either way: one device, on/off, house slow/fast. That rules out the ISP entirely.
Speed tests say 300 Mbps but my actual downloads crawl at like 5 MB/s and game updates take all night. Is the speed test lying to me?

Not lying, but measuring something narrower than you think — and watch the units first, because there's a real trap here: speeds are sold in megaBITS per second (Mbps) and downloads are usually shown in megaBYTES per second (MB/s). There are 8 bits in a byte, so 300 Mbps is at most ~37 MB/s. If you're seeing 5 MB/s, that's 40 Mbps — still far too slow, so there IS a problem, but the unit check recalibrates what 'right' looks like.

Now, why a test can say 300 while a real download crawls: speed tests connect to a nearby test server, often on your ISP's own network, using multiple parallel streams — ideal conditions. A game update comes from one content network, possibly far away, sometimes as a single stream, and the bottleneck can be that server, the path to it, or throttling of that traffic type. The discriminating test: download from two or three different sources (a different game's launcher, a large file from a major cloud provider) and run a second speed test on a different service, including one that tests single-stream. If everything except the speed test is slow, including wired and direct to the modem, gather times and sources and raise it with the ISP as a routing/peering issue. If one source is slow and others are fast, the source is the limit — frustrating, but no fault in your house, and no router upgrade will move it.

My fiber internet works great except my work VPN, which is unusably slow — everything through the VPN times out or crawls, but the same laptop is fine on my phone's hotspot. My IT department says it's my ISP. Are they right?

They might be, and there's a clean test that usually settles it — plus one home-side suspect to clear first. The hotspot comparison already tells us a lot: same laptop, same VPN, different network = fine. So the laptop and VPN configuration are probably innocent, and the difference lives in your home network or ISP path.

The home suspect is your router: some routers have 'security,' inspection, or VPN-passthrough quirks that mangle VPN traffic, and some mishandle the packet sizes VPNs use. Bisect it: connect the laptop directly to the fiber ONT/modem (router removed), restart things in order, and test the VPN. If the VPN is fast direct-to-ONT, your router is the culprit — look for firmware updates and try disabling advanced security/inspection features, or test with a different router. If the VPN is still slow with the router out of the picture, it genuinely is the ISP path (or the interaction between the ISP and your employer's VPN gateway), and IT's claim is supported.

Give IT the precise result either way: 'VPN slow on my fiber even wired directly to the ONT, fast on a hotspot, home network eliminated.' That sentence moves the problem to the right desk — and ask IT whether they see connection errors (like fragmentation or MTU issues) from your sessions, because a path that drops large packets breaks VPNs exactly this way while ordinary browsing survives.

Since a storm knocked our power out, the internet comes back but my router can't seem to get an address — restarting the router alone doesn't fix it; I have to restart the modem first, then the router. Why does the order matter?

Because the two devices have a conversation at startup, and order decides whether it happens. When your router boots, it asks the modem (really, through it, your ISP) for an internet address via DHCP. If the router asks while the modem is still booting and not yet passing traffic, the request goes nowhere — and many routers then wait a long time before asking again, or sit on a failed state. The modem also often remembers the last device it talked to and will only hand an address to that device until it restarts and forgets.

So the reliable sequence after an outage: modem (or ONT) first, wait until its lights show it's fully synced — usually two to five minutes, longer than feels necessary — then router, then everything else. The storm exposed this because both devices lost power and raced; the router won the race and lost the conversation.

If your power flickers often, a small UPS for the modem and router prevents the race entirely and also protects against the dips that corrupt router settings. And if the router repeatedly fails to recover even with correct ordering, check for a firmware update — graceful DHCP retry after a failed start is exactly the kind of bug vendors fix quietly.

I tested with my laptop plugged straight into the modem and got the full 600 Mbps I pay for. Through my router, same laptop, same cable, I get about 180. The router is only a year old. What's it doing to my speed?

That bypass test just saved you an argument with your ISP — the line delivers 600, and your router is where 420 of it goes. A year-old router should route 600 Mbps easily, so suspect configuration or one specific feature rather than raw weakness.

Work through the usual thieves: (1) QoS or bandwidth limiting — many routers have a QoS/SQM/'smart optimization' feature, and some ship with a manually set bandwidth cap left over from setup (a cap typed in for a previous, slower plan is a classic). Check those settings and either correct the numbers or disable QoS for a test. (2) Security/inspection features that process every packet in software. (3) The link itself — verify the router's WAN port negotiated 1000 Mbps, not 100; at 180 you're above that, so this is less likely here, but check anyway. (4) Hardware acceleration / NAT offload accidentally disabled by enabling a feature (some routers disable offload silently when you turn on traffic monitoring or parental controls).

Change one thing, retest wired through the router, repeat. If nothing restores it, factory-reset the router, set it up minimally (name, password, nothing else), and test before re-adding features — the feature that costs you 400 Mbps will identify itself when you re-enable it. If a bare, reset router still caps at ~180, its routing engine genuinely can't do more (some ISP-supplied boxes can't), and that's a hardware replacement case, with your bypass test as the proof it isn't the line.
My connection is fast but every hour or so the latency goes crazy for a couple of minutes — games rubber-band, calls glitch — then it's fine again. Speed tests between episodes are perfect.

Fast but periodically glitchy, on a roughly hourly rhythm, means something in your house wakes up on a schedule and floods the connection briefly — or something on the path does. The rhythm is the clue: backups, photo sync, security cameras uploading motion clips, a DVR, a cloud drive syncing a folder someone edits hourly, even a smart TV checking in with large telemetry — any of these can saturate your small upload pipe for two minutes, and during saturation, latency for everything else explodes (this is bufferbloat: queues fill, and your call packets wait behind bulk data).

Catch it in the act: run a continuous ping to your router and to a public address, and watch during a glitch. If ping to the router stays at 1-2 ms while the public ping spikes, the flood is crossing your internet link (house upload/download saturation). If even the router ping spikes, the flood is inside your Wi-Fi. Then check your router's traffic view at that moment — most show per-device usage live — or simply note what the clock says and what runs then.

Fixes: schedule the culprit for quiet hours or set its bandwidth limit (backup and sync tools all have one); if the culprit is legitimate and must run, a router with SQM/QoS (fq_codel or CAKE) keeps latency flat even under full load — it's the proper cure for bufferbloat. Quote the pattern if you must involve the ISP: 'hourly latency spikes to 300ms+ lasting ~2 minutes, throughput unaffected between episodes' — but exhaust the house suspects first, because this signature is domestic far more often than not.
My modem has a row of lights labeled DS, US, Online, and Link. The DS light has been blinking for an hour and there's no internet. What is it trying to tell me?

Those lights are the modem narrating its startup conversation with your ISP, and a blinking DS tells you exactly where the conversation stalled. DS is downstream: the modem is listening for the signal coming from the ISP. Solid means it found and locked onto it. Blinking for an hour means it is still searching — it cannot hear the ISP at all.

That localizes the fault to the physical path: the cable line into the modem, or the ISP's plant outside. Things to check yourself, in order: the coax connector on the modem and at the wall — snug, not just touching; any splitter between the wall and the modem (try removing it temporarily and connecting the modem to the wall feed directly — splitters fail and also eat signal); a different coax outlet if the house has one. Also confirm the outage isn't area-wide — the ISP's app or a neighbor — before spending more time.

If DS still won't lock with a direct wall connection, the fault is outside your control: no signal is arriving. Call the ISP and say the sentence that skips the script: 'Downstream light never locks, modem connected directly to the incoming line, no splitters.' US (upstream) blinking instead would mean it hears them but can't be heard back — a different fault, same phone call, different sentence.

Is there actually a difference between restarting my router and resetting it? My ISP's support told me to 'reset' it and now I'm nervous, because last time a tech reset something I lost all my settings.

Your nervousness is well placed — they're different operations with very different costs, and support scripts use the words loosely.

A restart (reboot, power cycle) is turning it off and on: unplug, wait 30 seconds, plug back in. All your settings survive — network name, password, everything. It clears temporary states: memory leaks, stuck processes, a bad negotiation with the modem. This is the safe, first move for almost every problem, and you can do it as often as needed.

A reset (factory reset) wipes the router back to how it left the factory: your Wi-Fi name and password revert to the defaults printed on the label, and any port forwarding, reservations, parental controls, or custom DNS vanish. Every device in the house then needs the (new-old) network details. It also erases the evidence of what was wrong, which is why it's a last resort, not a first step — and why a support agent suggesting it in minute two is skipping the diagnosis.

Rule of thumb: reboot freely; reset only when you've forgotten the admin password, when settings are corrupted beyond patient repair, or when you're starting fresh on purpose — and before resetting, photograph your settings screens if you can still log in. If your current problem is 'internet flaky,' reboot the modem first, then the router, in that order, and leave the reset button (and the paperclip) alone.
My fiber box has a red light labeled LOS and no internet since this morning. Restarting it didn't help. The ISP can't send anyone until Thursday. Is there anything at all I can check myself?

LOS means Loss Of Signal, and on fiber it has a precise meaning: the ONT (the fiber box) cannot see light coming from the ISP's equipment. Your restarts didn't help because the problem is optical and almost certainly outside your router settings — but there are two physical things genuinely worth checking, carefully.

First: the thin fiber cable. Trace it gently from the ONT to the wall jack. Fiber is glass — it must not be sharply bent, kinked, pinched under furniture, or pulled tight. If the outage followed vacuuming, furniture moving, or a pet incident, look there; a fiber bent past its limit or a connector nudged out of its socket produces exactly this. If a connector is visibly unseated, reseating it gently (it only fits one way, don't force it) is reasonable. Never look into the end of a fiber connector — the light is invisible and not eye-friendly.

Second: confirm nothing else in the chain lost power — the ONT's own power supply, any separate battery backup unit with a tripped state.

Beyond that, honestly, it's theirs: a cut or damaged drop cable, a fault at the street cabinet, or their equipment. When you call, the words that help are 'red LOS light, no light at the ONT, fiber run inspected for damage, connectors seated.' That tells the dispatcher it's a line fault, not a settings issue — and if a neighbor with the same provider is also down, say so; shared faults get restored as area events, not Thursday appointments.

I was trying to set up port forwarding for a home server and discovered my router's internet address starts with 100.64. A forum said this means I 'don't have a real IP address.' What does that mean and why does it break port forwarding?

The forum is right, and it's an increasingly common setup. Addresses starting 100.64 belong to a range reserved for CGNAT — Carrier-Grade NAT. Your ISP has run short of public IPv4 addresses, so instead of giving your router a public address of its own, they put many customers behind one shared public address. Your router does NAT (translating your home devices to its address), and the ISP does a second NAT above that (translating your router's 100.64 address to the shared public one).

Port forwarding breaks because a connection from the internet arrives at the ISP's shared public address, and the ISP's translator has no rule — and offers you no way to create one — to send it onward to your router. Your router's own forwarding rules are correct but unreachable; the door is behind another locked door.

How to confirm: compare the WAN address in your router (100.64.x.x) with what a 'what is my IP' site shows — if they differ, you're behind CGNAT. Options: ask your ISP for a public/static IP (some provide one free on request, some charge a small fee, some only on business plans — worth asking, and 'I need a public IPv4 for a home server, I'm behind CGNAT' is the exact ask); or sidestep inbound connections entirely with a VPN-based remote access service or a tunnel service that dials out from your server, which works fine through CGNAT. Ordinary browsing, streaming, and calls are unaffected — this only bites when you need the internet to knock on your door.
Every few weeks my router seems to reboot itself in the middle of the night — I wake up to find everything reconnected and the uptime reset. Is it dying, or is this normal?

A middle-of-the-night reboot every few weeks has three common explanations, and only one of them is dying. First, the innocent one: many ISPs push firmware updates and maintenance reboots to their supplied routers in the small hours, and some routers have a scheduled-reboot feature enabled by default or by a previous setup. Second: a watchdog — the router detects a hung process and restarts itself rather than staying broken, which is the feature working as designed, if slightly too often. Third, the worrying one: heat or a marginal power supply causing crashes that happen to surface at night because nobody notices them in the day.

Discriminate by pattern and paperwork: check the router's admin page after a reboot — firmware version changes point to pushed updates; a log entry like 'scheduled reboot' or a settings page with a reboot schedule settles it. Check whether uptime resets happen at a consistent time (3:00-4:00am smells like maintenance; random times smell like crashes). Feel the router: uncomfortably hot, in a closed cabinet, or stacked on the modem suggests giving it air and seeing if the reboots stop. And swap the power adapter if you have an identical one — a sagging adapter causes exactly this and is cheap to eliminate.

If reboots are weekly-ish, at random times, with a cool router and no update history, treat it as failing hardware and replace it on your schedule rather than its.

I have my ISP's modem-router combo and I added my own router behind it. Now some things are weird: my game console complains about 'NAT type,' and a couple of smart devices are unreachable from my phone. A friend said 'double NAT.' What's actually happening?

Your friend is right, and the weirdness pattern fits perfectly. NAT is the translation your router does between your home network's private addresses and your one internet address. With two routers in a chain, translation happens twice, and your devices now live on two different home networks: some on the ISP box's network, some on your router's network. Those two networks can't freely see each other, which is why the phone (on one) can't reach devices (on the other), and the console's 'NAT type' complaint is it detecting the double translation, which breaks some game and voice features.

Confirm by checking addresses: a device on your router should get an address like 192.168.1.x from it, while your router's own internet/WAN address will be another private address (like 192.168.0.x) handed out by the ISP box — a private WAN address is the fingerprint of double NAT.

Fixes, best first: (1) Put the ISP box into bridge/passthrough mode so it acts as a pure modem and your router gets the real internet address — one network, one NAT. The ISP can enable this or tell you the menu path. (2) Or do the opposite: retire your router's routing — set it to access-point mode and let the ISP box run the one network. (3) The half-measure: plug everything into your router only, and nothing (except the router) into the ISP box; this hides the split-brain problem but keeps double NAT for gaming. Pick option 1 if you like your router's features; option 2 if you don't care.
My DSL internet drops out every time the landline phone rings or someone makes a call. It reconnects a minute later. This started recently and nothing about my setup changed, as far as I know.

DSL and voice share the same copper pair, separated by frequency — voice low, DSL high — and little filters (microfilters, or a splitter at the entry point) keep them out of each other's way. 'Drops when the phone rings' is the textbook symptom of that separation failing: the ring signal is a hefty voltage spike, and if it leaks into the DSL frequencies, the modem loses sync and retrains, which takes about the minute you're seeing.

'Nothing changed' usually means a filter died rather than being removed — they fail quietly. The discriminating test: unplug every phone, answering machine, and fax from every socket, leaving only the modem connected (ideally at the master socket), then call your landline from a mobile. If the modem holds sync through the ring with all phones disconnected, the line and modem are fine and one of the disconnected items or its filter is the culprit. Reconnect items one at a time, ringing after each, and the drop will name its cause.

If it drops even with everything unplugged and the modem alone at the master socket, the fault is the line or the entry splitter — that's the ISP's side, and your evidence is strong: 'sync drops on ring, reproduced with all extensions disconnected at the master socket.' Don't let them send you a new router for that. And if the culprit turns out to be a filter, replace filters on every socket that has a phone device — they're cheap, and their siblings are the same age.

My router keeps losing the correct time — it thinks it's 2019 after every power blip, and my parental-control schedules and 'internet off at bedtime' rules fire at crazy times until it sorts itself out. Sometimes it never sorts itself out.

Routers don't have a battery-backed clock like a PC; after a power loss they boot up with a factory default date and must fetch the real time from the internet (NTP) before schedules make sense. When yours stays in 2019, the time fetch is failing — and the usual reason is a chicken-and-egg problem: the router needs working DNS to find the time server by name, and if its DNS or internet connection isn't up yet when it tries, some routers give up instead of retrying.

Things to check: in the admin settings, find the time/NTP section — confirm NTP is enabled and try setting the time server to a numeric address or a well-known pool (pool.ntp.org) and your correct timezone (schedules fire wrong also when the timezone is right-time-wrong-zone). Check whether the problem correlates with the router booting before the modem is ready: if the router asks for time before the internet exists and never retries, the practical fix is the boot order — modem first, fully synced, then router — or a small UPS so the router never loses power in the first place.

Also update the firmware: 'NTP never retries after boot' is a classic quietly-fixed bug. If time is correct but schedules still fire oddly, re-check whether the rules use the router's timezone or were created under a daylight-saving assumption — recreate one rule fresh and compare behavior before rebuilding them all.
I set up the guest Wi-Fi for visitors, and now my brother-in-law, staying with us for a month, can't print to our printer or see our shared drive from the guest network. Did I break something?

You didn't break anything — the guest network is doing exactly the job it was built for. A guest network is deliberately isolated: devices on it can reach the internet but are fenced off from your main network, so a visitor's compromised laptop can't wander into your files, and your printer and shared drive are invisible to it on purpose. The 'problem' is that a month-long resident is not really a guest in the security sense.

You have three honest options. (1) Move his devices to the main network — simplest, appropriate if you trust his devices as you'd trust your own; that's a judgment call about his laptop hygiene, not a technical one. (2) Some routers offer a setting like 'allow guests to access local network' or a per-device exception — if yours does, enabling it just for the printer is a middle path, though it weakens the fence for everyone on the guest network, not just him. (3) Work around it: he emails documents to you for printing, or the printer's own cloud/email-print feature (many printers accept jobs via a vendor service that crosses the fence legitimately, since both sides reach the internet).

What not to do: don't disable the guest isolation permanently just to fix a temporary stay, and don't move the printer onto the guest network — that inverts the design and strands your own devices instead. When he leaves, nothing needs undoing if you chose option 1 or 3 beyond, if you like, changing the main password.

My ISP keeps blaming my 'old modem' for my speed problems and wants me to rent theirs. My modem is four years old but supports speeds well above my plan on paper. How do I know if they're right or just upselling?

Make them prove it with the test that removes all doubt: the wired bypass at the demarcation point. Connect a computer directly to your modem, run speed tests at a couple of times of day, and also pull the modem's own status page — for cable, that's usually 192.168.100.1, showing per-channel downstream power and SNR, upstream power, and error counters.

Interpretation: healthy cable downstream power sits roughly between -7 and +7 dBmV (acceptable to about ±10), SNR above ~35 dB, upstream power below ~50 dBmV, and uncorrectable errors near zero. If your levels are in range and the direct-to-modem wired test still can't reach plan speed at off-peak hours, the modem is very likely innocent and the limit is their provisioning or plant — a rented modem would inherit the same line. If levels are out of range, that's also a line problem, not a modem problem — modems report the line; they don't create it.

Where the ISP can be right: if your plan's speed tier uses channel bonding or a newer standard (like DOCSIS 3.1) that your modem lacks, the modem genuinely caps you — check your plan's fine print against the modem's spec sheet, that's a paper comparison, not a sales call. And if the modem's error log shows it rebooting or losing sync, age may be real. So: levels + logs + direct test. If all three are clean, decline the rental politely and quote your numbers — 'direct to my modem, wired, 3pm, I get X of Y, levels are [values], uncorrectables zero' is a sentence upsells don't survive.
After I updated my router's firmware, half my smart-home devices stopped connecting, though phones and laptops are fine. The update was supposed to be routine. What did it change?

Firmware updates sometimes change default security settings, and smart-home devices are the canaries: phones and laptops support the newest Wi-Fi security (WPA3), while many plugs, bulbs, and cameras only speak the older WPA2 — and some handle the mixed WPA2/WPA3 transition mode badly. An update that flipped your security mode, or enabled a feature like band steering or 'smart connect' by default, produces exactly your pattern: modern devices fine, simple devices exiled.

Discriminating test: check the router's wireless security setting. If it now says WPA3 or WPA2/WPA3 mixed, set it explicitly to WPA2 (AES) and see if the devices return. Also check whether the update renamed or merged your networks (a combined single name replacing separate 2.4/5 names confuses devices that were joined to a specific band) and whether a 'minimum RSSI' or client-isolation feature appeared.

If security mode is the culprit, you face a real trade-off, so make it deliberately: WPA2 with a long, unique password is still respectable security for a home; the devices are a bigger risk through their cloud accounts than through your Wi-Fi encryption. A cleaner long-term answer some routers offer is a separate IoT network pinned to WPA2/2.4 GHz, keeping the main network on WPA3. And note the update's other lesson: before the next firmware update, export the router's configuration backup — restoring settings beats rediscovering them.
Windows says my printer is 'offline' but the printer is on, connected to Wi-Fi, and its little screen shows our network name. I can print from my phone just fine. Why does the PC insist it's offline?

Phone prints, PC says offline, printer demonstrably on the network: the fault is in how the PC talks to the printer, not in the printer. The usual mechanism: Windows often installs network printers using an automatic WSD port or a snapshot of the printer's address. If the printer's IP address has changed since (router reboot, new router, lease expired), the phone — which rediscovers the printer fresh each time by name — finds it, while the PC keeps knocking on the old address and declaring it offline.

Confirm it: find the printer's current IP address (print a network configuration page from the printer's menu, or look in your router's connected-devices list), then try to open that address in the PC's browser — most printers show a status page. If it loads, the printer is reachable and the PC's printer definition is stale.

Fix properly rather than temporarily: in Windows, remove the printer and re-add it, and if you're comfortable, add it by its IP address; then stop the address from wandering — in your router, reserve that IP for the printer (a DHCP reservation tied to the printer), so the PC's definition stays true forever. Also untick 'use printer offline' if it got set (right-click the printer queue — it happens accidentally more often than anyone admits). The phone working was the key evidence all along: it proved the printer and network innocent in one stroke.
Ever since we got a new router, the printer vanished from our computers. It says it's connected to Wi-Fi — the new network name, we re-entered the password — but no computer can find it.

The printer probably did join the new network — with a new address, and possibly on a different corner of it than your computers expect. A new router means a new DHCP server handing out addresses, sometimes on a different scheme (the old router may have used 192.168.0.x, the new one 192.168.1.x), and computers that had the printer installed by its old address are now pointing at a stranger's house, so to speak.

Also check the sneakier possibility: the new router's setup left the printer on a guest or IoT network, or the computers on a band where the router isolates devices ('AP isolation' is sometimes on by default for the new router's extra networks). Printer discovery (Bonjour/AirPrint and Windows discovery) doesn't cross those fences.

Methodical fix: (1) Print the printer's network configuration page — it shows its current IP address and network name. Confirm the network name matches the one the computers use, exactly. (2) From a computer, ping that IP or open it in a browser; the printer's status page should load. If it doesn't load despite matching network names, suspect isolation settings in the new router. (3) Once reachable, remove and re-add the printer on each computer so they learn the new address, and set a DHCP reservation for the printer in the new router so the address stops moving. The printer telling you 'connected' was true — it was just connected at a new address, in a house whose other residents had the old one written down.

My printer prints test pages and documents from my phone perfectly, but from my Windows PC everything comes out garbled — weird characters, or it prints dozens of pages of nonsense from a one-page document.

A printer that renders its own test page and phone jobs perfectly but garbles PC jobs has a driver problem, full stop — the printer's hardware and network are proven good by the phone, and the nonsense-pages symptom is the classic signature of the PC sending data in a language the printer doesn't speak (wrong driver, or a generic driver guessing the wrong page-description language: PCL vs PostScript vs the vendor's own).

Confirm by checking what driver the PC is using: in the printer properties, note the driver name. If it's a generic class driver or a driver for a different model (a common souvenir of Windows automatically 'finding' the printer), that's your culprit.

Fix: install the manufacturer's own current driver for your exact model and operating system from the vendor's site, remove the old printer entry, and re-add it using the new driver. Then print the same one-page document that produced the garbage. While you're in settings, note the driver type — if the vendor offers both PCL and PostScript variants, PCL is the safer default for office documents. Don't throw away the garbled stack as a total loss: it's actually useful evidence — if garbling returns after a Windows update, the update swapped your driver again, which happens, and reinstalling the vendor driver is the same fix.
There's a print job stuck in my queue from yesterday and now nothing prints — everything I send just lines up behind it. The printer itself seems fine. How do I unstick this?

The queue lives on your computer, not the printer — one corrupt or stalled job at the front blocks every job behind it, like a stalled car in a single-lane tunnel. The printer is fine; your PC's print spooler (the service that manages the queue) is holding the wreck.

Escalate gently: first, open the print queue, select the stuck job, and cancel it. Give it a full minute — cancellation of a truly wedged job is slow. If it sits at 'deleting' forever, restart the spooler: on Windows, open Services, find 'Print Spooler,' and restart it (or restart the PC, which does the same thing less surgically). The queue should clear entirely — you'll lose the jobs behind the stuck one too and need to resend them, which is why you try the gentle cancel first.

If one particular document re-wedges the queue every time you print it, the document itself is the fault — a damaged PDF or a pathological page. Test by printing a simple text file first, then the document; if only that file jams things, print it from a different program or re-save/export it fresh. And note the pattern for the future: 'printer fine, nothing prints, jobs piling up' is always the queue, never the printer — check the queue before touching any printer settings.

Our office printer takes five minutes to print a big PDF, spooling forever, but small documents print instantly. It's a decent laser printer on a wired connection. What's slow — the network, the printer, or the file?

Almost certainly the file and how it's rendered, not the network — a wired connection moves even a fat print job in seconds, while a complex PDF (scanned images, layered graphics, embedded fonts) must be converted into the printer's page language, and that conversion happens either slowly on your PC (spooling) or slowly in the printer's modest processor.

Bisect it: (1) Watch the spool size — if a 2 MB PDF becomes a 400 MB spool file, your PC is rendering it into a giant bitmap-ish stream; that's the 'spooling forever' you see. (2) Try 'Print as image' in the PDF reader's advanced options — counterintuitively this sometimes fixes pathological files by simplifying what the driver must interpret; if it flies, the original file's structure was the problem. (3) Try the other driver language if your printer offers both PCL and PostScript — complex PDFs often render dramatically faster on one than the other; it's a five-minute experiment. (4) Print the same file from a different computer: if it's fast there, your PC's driver or its settings (like a forced 1200 dpi or 'let the printer determine color' toggles) are the difference.

What not to conclude: that the network or the printer is dying. Small jobs instant + big jobs slow + wired connection is a rendering story almost every time, and the fix is in the driver/file layer, not in cables or a new printer.

My printer used to scan to email fine, but it stopped working last month with a vague 'server error.' I didn't change anything on the printer. The email provider is one of the big ones. What probably happened?

Something changed — just not on your side of the fence. Scan-to-email makes the printer log into a mail server like a tiny email client, using settings and a password stored in the printer. The big providers have been steadily retiring basic password sign-in for third-party devices and requiring stronger methods (app-specific passwords or modern OAuth sign-in). When a provider flips that switch, every printer using the old method starts failing with exactly your vague error, on a random Tuesday, with no change at home.

Check the provider's side first: sign in to your account on the web and look for security notices about third-party/app access, and check whether the account now requires two-step verification (enabling it often invalidates the old password for devices). The supported path on many setups is generating an app-specific password in your account's security settings and entering that into the printer's email settings — use the provider's own account pages for this; never type your main account password into unfamiliar sites or share it anywhere.

If your printer is older and only supports the retired method with no app-password option, the honest workarounds are the vendor's scan-to-computer or scan-to-cloud feature, or scanning to a USB/network folder instead. And if the printer shows a more specific error code in its web settings page (the one you reach via its IP address), note it — 'authentication failed' versus 'cannot reach server' point in opposite directions: credentials versus network/DNS.
My printer used to offer two-sided printing and now the option is just gone from the print dialog. I didn't remove anything. It still prints fine otherwise.

The duplexer didn't fall off — its description did. The print dialog shows options the driver believes the printer has. When Windows (or an update) swaps your vendor driver for a generic class driver, the generic driver knows the printer can print but not that it has a duplex unit, finishing options, or extra trays — so those options quietly vanish from the dialog while basic printing carries on. This is one of the most common post-update printer mysteries.

Confirm: open the printer's properties and look at the driver name. If it says something generic ('class driver,' a Microsoft IPP driver) rather than the manufacturer's model-specific driver, that's it. There's also a settings-level version of this: in the vendor driver's device settings tab, the duplex unit may be listed as 'not installed' — flipping it to 'installed' restores the option without reinstalling anything.

Fix: install the manufacturer's current driver for your exact model, remove the old entry, re-add the printer on the new driver, and check the dialog — duplex should be back. To reduce repeats, note that big OS updates are the usual swap moment; if the option vanishes again after one, you already know the five-minute cure.
Our label printer prints completely blank labels — the printer feeds and 'prints,' but nothing is on them. It worked last week. We did get a new box of labels.

New labels plus blank output is a strong lead, because label printers are sensitive to what they're fed in a way page printers aren't. Two main suspects. First: the labels themselves. Direct-thermal printers print by heating coated label stock — if the new box is thermal-transfer stock (or vice versa, the printer expects a ribbon), the printhead has nothing to react with and you get perfect blanks. The scratch test discriminates instantly: run a fingernail firmly across a label — direct-thermal stock shows a dark mark. If no mark, the stock isn't direct-thermal.

Second: size/sensor mismatch. If the new labels are a different size or the gap/black-mark position differs, the printer may be 'printing' onto the gap or misreading where each label starts — output can land between labels or not at all. The fix there is a media calibration (most label printers have a feed-button hold procedure that measures the stock) plus confirming the label size in the driver matches the physical stock — driver says 4x6 while the roll is 2x1 produces all kinds of wrong, including apparent blanks.

Check the fingernail test first — it takes two seconds and separates chemistry from configuration. And keep one known-good label from the old roll as a reference standard; with consumables, 'worked last week, new box this week' should always make the new box prove its innocence.
My wireless printer keeps disappearing from the network a few hours after I use it. Restarting the printer brings it back for a while. It's like it falls asleep and never wakes up.

That's close to literally what's happening: the printer's power-saving sleep is dropping its Wi-Fi connection, and it isn't rejoining cleanly on wake. Two mechanisms combine — the printer's radio sleeps deeply and misses the network, and/or its DHCP lease (its rented address) expires while it sleeps, so when it half-wakes it's at a stale address or no address, invisible to your computers.

Test the theory: when it's 'disappeared,' check whether the printer's own screen shows Wi-Fi connected and what address it claims; then look for that address in the router's client list. If the printer thinks it's connected but the router doesn't list it, the radio wake-up is failing. If it's listed at a different address than your computers expect, the address-drift half of the problem is yours.

Fixes, cumulative: give the printer a DHCP reservation (or a static address) in the router so its address can never drift; in the printer's settings, look for Wi-Fi power management / sleep options — many have an 'auto off' that's more aggressive than the plain sleep, and disabling auto-off while keeping sleep often cures it; update the printer's firmware, since wake-from-sleep radio bugs are a staple of printer firmware fixes. If your router has a 'band steering' or airtime-fairness feature, try the printer pinned to 2.4 GHz — sleepy radios roam badly. Judge over a week, not an hour: the failure needs idle time to declare itself.

My iPhone used to find our printer with AirPrint, but since we got a mesh Wi-Fi system it says 'No AirPrint printers found' — even though the printer is connected and prints from our Mac (which found it once we typed in its address).

The Mac succeeding by typed address while AirPrint discovery fails is the diagnostic gold here: the printer is on the network and reachable — what's broken is discovery. AirPrint relies on Bonjour (mDNS), which broadcasts announcements that, by design, don't cross network boundaries. Mesh systems create boundary traps: if the printer joined one segment (say, a node's separate subnet in a misconfigured double-router mesh, or the guest/IoT network) and the iPhone sits on another, the two can still sometimes route traffic by address, but the discovery broadcasts never meet.

Checklist: (1) Confirm the printer and iPhone are on the same network name and, in the mesh app, the same network segment — not guest, not IoT-isolated. (2) Confirm the mesh is in the right mode: if your mesh is running as a second router behind your ISP router, you have double NAT and a split network; putting the mesh in bridge/access-point mode unifies it. (3) In the mesh settings, look for toggles that block multicast/mDNS or isolate clients, sometimes labeled as IoT protection — discovery needs multicast allowed within the network. (4) Restart order once things are consistent: printer last, so it announces itself into the settled network.

Test by standing near a different mesh node — if AirPrint works near one node and not another, the nodes aren't one happy network yet, and that's the vendor's app settings (or bridge mode) rather than the printer.
Right after a big Windows update, all my prints started coming out faded and draft-looking, with a 'toner save' feel. The cartridge is half full. Did the update really do that, or is it coincidence?

It plausibly did — and there's a two-minute test that separates the update's settings from the cartridge's health. Print a test or demo page using only the printer's own buttons/menus, no computer involved. That page is generated by the printer itself. If the internal test page is rich and dark, the printer and cartridge are fine and the faintness lives in what the computer is sending — the update's doing. If the internal page is also faded, the computer is innocent and you're back to cartridge/drum causes.

The mechanism, when it's the update: updates can replace the vendor driver with a generic one or reset driver preferences, and default profiles often enable 'EconoMode / toner save / draft quality' or drop the print quality from its previous setting to a lower default. Open the printer properties → printing preferences and look at quality and economy settings; restore 'best/normal' quality and turn off any toner-save toggle, then reprint the same page that looked washed out.

Half-full cartridge plus sudden change plus a big update in the same week: trust the timeline. Hardware fades gradually; settings change overnight. Keep the internal test page trick in your pocket — it bisects 'the printer' from 'the computer' for almost every quality complaint, forever.

I read my cable modem's status page like a forum suggested. Downstream power is around -13 dBmV on most channels, SNR is 31 dB, and there are millions of 'uncorrectable' errors. My internet mostly works but drops a few times a day. The ISP phone agent said 'signal looks fine.' Who's right?

You are, and the numbers you quoted are the proof. For cable (DOCSIS), the generally accepted healthy ranges are: downstream power between about -7 and +7 dBmV (workable to roughly ±10, marginal beyond), downstream SNR at least 35-36 dB for the higher-order modulations modern plans use, and uncorrectable errors essentially at zero — a handful over weeks, not millions. At -13 dBmV your modem is straining to hear a weak signal; at 31 dB SNR the signal it hears is noisy; millions of uncorrectables mean data is arriving damaged beyond repair and must be re-sent, which matches your drops exactly.

This combination — weak AND noisy with massive uncorrectables — points at the physical plant: a failing or excess splitter, a corroded outdoor connector, water in a fitting, a chewed line, or a bad drop from the pole. Your modem can't fix any of those, and neither can a new modem; a replacement would report the same numbers.

Do the one premises check available to you: connect the modem directly to the incoming line where it enters the house (no splitters, no extra outlets) and re-read the levels. If they jump into range, the fault is your inside wiring/splitter — yours to fix. If they're still -13/31 at the entry point, the fault is the ISP's, definitively. Then escalate past the script with the sentence: 'At the demarc, downstream -13 dBmV, SNR 31, uncorrectables in the millions — this is a plant problem, please book a line tech, not a modem swap.' Numbers end arguments that adjectives can't.

We have a small office with one printer shared by six people. Since we replaced our router, prints from two of the PCs go to the printer fine, but the other four print to... nothing. No error, jobs just vanish. All six PCs are on the same Wi-Fi name.

Jobs vanishing without errors, on some PCs but not others, after a router change: think addresses and subnets, not printer faults. The likeliest story: the new router hands out addresses in a different range than the old one, and the four failing PCs still have the printer installed at its old address — but they'd usually error, not vanish. Vanishing suggests the jobs ARE being accepted somewhere: possibly an identically-named printer object on those PCs pointing at a software/virtual port, or those PCs are actually on a different segment of the new setup (a second SSID with the same name from an old extender still running, putting them on a different subnet where a stale route eats the jobs).

Discriminate per PC: on a working and a failing PC, compare (a) the IP address each PC itself has — same range? (b) the printer port address in printer properties — same target? Print a network config page from the printer for its true current address. Any mismatch names the fault.

Then rebuild uniformly: remove the printer from all six PCs, reserve a fixed address for the printer in the router, and re-add it everywhere by that address. Kill the zombie extender if that's what you find — old range extenders rebroadcasting the same name are a classic post-upgrade haunting. Finish with a test page from each PC, one at a time, and watch it physically emerge; 'no error' has already lied to you once in this story.
